scenarios.context: A student asks her tutor how to describe a graph in English.

speakerA.en: Could you help me describe this line graph? It shows how the number of students in a city changed between 2010 and 2020.
So I could say that the number of students rose steadily over the decade?
It went up until 2015, then dropped slightly, and finally recovered.
Which verbs should I use for changes? I keep repeating "increase".
And adverbs like "sharply" and "gradually" would show how fast it changed?
That helps a lot. Could I also compare it with the second graph?

speakerB.en: Of course. First, give an overview. Say what the general trend is before you mention any figures.
Yes, but check the details. Did it increase continuously, or were there any fluctuations?
Then you could write that it peaked in 2015 before declining briefly and then climbing again.
Try "rise", "grow" and "climb" for upward movements, and "fall", "decline" and "drop" for downward ones.
Exactly. Use "sharply" for a big change in a short time and "gradually" for a slow one.
Yes, point out the main similarities and differences, and support them with a few figures.

scenarios.context: Two students revise statistics for a test.

speakerA.en: This question asks for the mean, median and mode of the test scores. I always mix them up.
And the median is the middle value once the scores are arranged in order?
What about the mode?
Why would we use the median instead of the mean?
That's a useful example. So the median gives a fairer picture of a typical value.
The range is the difference between the highest and lowest scores, so it's thirty-two.

speakerB.en: The mean is the average, so you add all the scores and divide by the number of students.
Correct. If there's an even number of scores, you take the mean of the two middle ones.
It's simply the value that appears most often. A set of data can have more than one mode.
Because extreme values affect the mean. For example, one very high salary can make a company seem richer than it is.
In that case, yes. Now try the second part, where you have to find the range and comment on the spread.
Right. A large range means that the results are widely spread, so the class is quite uneven.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about the chances of winning the lottery.

speakerA.en: My uncle buys a lottery ticket every week. He says that sooner or later he's bound to win.
But if the chance of winning is one in ten million, doesn't it get more likely the more he plays?
So in probability terms, is it a bad investment?
Then why do people keep playing?
That reminds me of people who are afraid of flying but never worry about driving.
I'll explain that to my uncle, although I doubt that it will change his mind.

speakerB.en: That's a common misunderstanding. Each draw is independent, so the past results don't affect the next one.
It increases slightly with every ticket, but it remains tiny. He'd spend far more money than he would ever win.
In terms of expected value, yes. On average, players lose money, which is how the lottery makes a profit.
Partly because of the excitement, and partly because we tend to overestimate unlikely events.
Exactly. Statistically, driving is far more dangerous, but vivid news stories make plane crashes seem more common.
Probably not, but at least you'll have used your maths for something practical.

scenarios.context: Two students compare two savings accounts for a maths project.

speakerA.en: We've been asked to compare two savings accounts. One pays simple interest, and the other pays compound interest.
With simple interest, you only earn interest on the original amount. With compound interest, you also earn it on the interest you've already received.
Yes, especially over a long period. If you invest one thousand pounds at five percent for twenty years, you get much more with compound interest.
Right. You multiply by one point zero five each year, so after twenty years the total is about two thousand six hundred and fifty pounds.
That's why starting to save early matters so much, even if the amounts are small.
Exactly, which is why it's dangerous to carry a balance from month to month.

speakerB.en: What's the difference? The names sound similar, but I assume the results aren't.
So the money grows faster with compound interest?
Let me calculate it. After one year it's one thousand and fifty, and then the next year is five percent of that new total.
That's considerably more than simple interest, which would only give two thousand.
And it works the other way round with debts, doesn't it? Interest on credit cards grows in the same way.
Now I understand why my parents keep telling me to avoid borrowing money for things I don't need.

scenarios.context: Two friends question an advertisement that quotes survey results.

speakerA.en: Look at this headline: "Nine out of ten dentists recommend our toothpaste." It sounds convincing, doesn't it?
And who chose them? If the company selected them, the sample wouldn't be representative.
Another thing I've noticed is that graphs can be misleading when the vertical axis doesn't start at zero.
What about the difference between correlation and causation?
That's a funny example, but it makes the point clearly.
I'll make a checklist to help me remember all of those points.

speakerB.en: It does, but I'd want to know how many dentists were asked. Perhaps they only questioned ten.
Exactly. A good survey needs a large, random sample so that the results reflect the whole population.
Yes, a small difference can look enormous if the scale is cut off. Always check the axes before you draw conclusions.
Two things can rise together without one causing the other. Ice cream sales and sunburn both increase in summer, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn.
In an exam, you may be asked to criticise a statement like this, so mention the sample size, the source and possible bias.
Good idea. It will also help you in everyday life when you read the news.
